title: Evolution & Speciation
description: Natural selection, fitness, modes of selection, sexual selection, gene flow, homology, species concepts, reproductive barriers, speciation and cladistics.

cards.title: What conditions must hold for natural selection to change a population over generations?
cards.body:
Heritable variation in a trait, more offspring than can survive, and differences in survival and reproduction tied to that trait.

Individuals vary, some of that variation is **heritable**, and some heritable traits improve survival and reproduction. Favored traits then become more common over generations.

Key idea: selection acts on individuals' phenotypes, but **populations** are what evolve.
cards.searchQuery: conditions for natural selection heritable variation differential reproduction

cards.title: A strong, long-lived male mouse never fathers any offspring. What is his relative fitness?
cards.body:
Zero.

**Relative fitness** is an individual's contribution to the gene pool of the next generation compared with others' contributions.

Watch out: strength and long life count only insofar as they lead to offspring.
cards.searchQuery: relative fitness definition reproductive success zero offspring

cards.title: After a drought left mostly large, hard seeds, finches with deeper beaks survived and mean beak depth rose. What mode of selection is this?
cards.body:
Directional selection.

Individuals at **one extreme** of a trait are favored, so the population's mean shifts in that direction.

Example: medium ground finches on Daphne Major (Galápagos) after the 1977 drought. The survivors' offspring had deeper beaks on average.
cards.searchQuery: directional selection Daphne Major finches beak depth drought

cards.title: Babies of intermediate birth weight have historically survived better than very small or very large ones. What mode of selection is this?
cards.body:
Stabilizing selection.

It favors **intermediate phenotypes** and acts against both extremes, so variation shrinks while the mean stays about the same.

Example: most human birth weights fall around $3$–$4\,\mathrm{kg}$. Much smaller or larger babies have had higher mortality.
cards.searchQuery: stabilizing selection human birth weight intermediate phenotype

cards.title: Seedcracker finches with small or large beaks feed efficiently, but those with intermediate beaks don't. What mode of selection is this?
cards.body:
Disruptive selection.

Both **extremes** are favored over intermediates, which can split a trait into two peaks.

Example: in black-bellied seedcrackers in Cameroon, small-billed birds feed mainly on soft seeds and large-billed birds crack hard ones. Intermediate bills handle both poorly.
cards.searchQuery: disruptive selection black-bellied seedcracker bill size

cards.title: Peahens prefer to mate with the males that have the showiest tails. What specific form of sexual selection is this?
cards.body:
Intersexual selection (mate choice).

Members of one sex, usually females, **choose mates** based on certain traits. Contrast **intrasexual selection**: competition within one sex, often males, for mates.

Watch out: either form can spread traits that boost mating success even if they reduce survival. This produces sexual dimorphism.
cards.searchQuery: intersexual selection mate choice peahen tail sexual selection

cards.title: What is the movement of alleles into or out of a population by migrating fertile individuals or their gametes, such as pollen, called?
cards.body:
Gene flow.

It tends to make populations **more genetically alike**. It can spread useful alleles, such as insecticide resistance among mosquito populations, or swamp local adaptations.

Watch out: gene flow is not the same as genetic drift, which is chance change in allele frequencies and is strongest in small populations.
cards.searchQuery: gene flow definition alleles migration between populations

cards.title: How do homologous structures differ from analogous structures? Give an example of each.
cards.body:
Homologous: similar because of **shared ancestry**. Analogous: similar in function but evolved independently.

Homologous example: the human arm, whale flipper and bat wing share the same set of bones despite different functions. Analogous example: bird wings and insect wings, which arose by **convergent evolution**.

Key idea: homologies indicate common ancestry; analogies don't.
cards.searchQuery: homologous vs analogous structures convergent evolution examples

cards.title: Remnants of structures that were functional in an organism's ancestors, like the pelvic bones of some snakes, are called what?
cards.body:
Vestigial structures.

They persist because they are inherited from ancestors that used them, so they are evidence of **descent with modification**.

They may keep minor uses. What matters is that they are reduced leftovers of an ancestral feature, like the reduced eyes of blind cave fish.
cards.searchQuery: vestigial structures snake pelvic bones evidence of evolution

cards.title: According to the biological species concept, what makes two populations members of the same species?
cards.body:
They can interbreed in nature and produce viable, fertile offspring, and they are reproductively isolated from other such groups.

The **biological species concept** focuses on gene flow within a species and barriers between species.

Watch out: it can't be applied to fossils or to asexual organisms such as prokaryotes, so morphological, ecological and phylogenetic species concepts are used as well.
cards.searchQuery: biological species concept definition reproductive isolation limitations

cards.title: Eastern spotted skunks mate in late winter, western spotted skunks in late summer, so they don't interbreed. Which specific barrier is this?
cards.body:
Temporal isolation.

It is a **prezygotic** barrier: it acts before fertilization. Other prezygotic barriers are habitat, behavioral, mechanical and gametic isolation.

Key idea: **postzygotic** barriers act after a hybrid zygote forms: reduced hybrid viability, reduced hybrid fertility and hybrid breakdown.
cards.searchQuery: temporal isolation spotted skunks prezygotic barrier

cards.title: A horse and a donkey can produce a mule, but mules are sterile. What type of reproductive barrier is this?
cards.body:
A postzygotic barrier: reduced hybrid fertility.

The hybrid forms and survives but can't reproduce, because the parents' chromosomes differ in number and structure and can't pair properly in meiosis.

Key idea: the other postzygotic barriers are **reduced hybrid viability** and **hybrid breakdown**, where later-generation hybrids are feeble or sterile.
cards.searchQuery: postzygotic barrier mule reduced hybrid fertility

cards.title: What is the key difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation?
cards.body:
Allopatric: a **geographic barrier** splits a population. Sympatric: a new species arises in the same area with no geographic barrier.

Allopatric example: snapping shrimp populations separated by the Isthmus of Panama diverged into distinct species.

Sympatric speciation can occur through polyploidy, habitat differentiation or sexual selection.
cards.searchQuery: allopatric vs sympatric speciation difference geographic barrier

cards.title: A cell-division error gives a plant extra chromosome sets, isolating it from its parent species in one generation. What is this condition?
cards.body:
Polyploidy.

A tetraploid ($4n$) can self-pollinate or mate with other tetraploids. Crosses with its diploid parents give triploid offspring with reduced fertility, so it is **reproductively isolated at once**.

Example: wheat, oats, cotton and potatoes are polyploids. It is a common route to sympatric speciation in plants.
cards.searchQuery: polyploidy sympatric speciation plants tetraploid

cards.title: Hair is found in all mammals and in no other vertebrates. In cladistic terms, what kind of character is hair for the mammal clade?
cards.body:
A shared derived character (synapomorphy).

It is an evolutionary novelty unique to a clade, so it can **define that clade**. A clade is an ancestor plus all of its descendants.

Watch out: a backbone is a shared **ancestral** character for mammals. It arose in an earlier ancestor and is shared with other vertebrates.
cards.searchQuery: shared derived character synapomorphy hair mammals cladistics

cards.title: How does the punctuated equilibrium model of the tempo of speciation differ from gradualism?
cards.body:
Punctuated equilibrium: species appear **relatively suddenly** in the fossil record, then change little for long periods (stasis). Gradualism: species diverge slowly and steadily through many intermediate forms.

Watch out: "sudden" in geologic time can still mean tens of thousands of years. The fossil record shows both patterns.
cards.searchQuery: punctuated equilibrium vs gradualism tempo of speciation stasis

cards.title: On which ship did Charles Darwin sail around the world from 1831 to 1836, collecting observations that shaped his ideas?
cards.body:
HMS Beagle.

Darwin was the ship's naturalist. His observations of South American fossils and of Galápagos species helped him develop the idea of **descent with modification**.

Tip: he published On the Origin of Species only in 1859, more than two decades after the voyage ended.
cards.searchQuery: Darwin HMS Beagle voyage 1831 1836 naturalist

cards.title: What phrase did Darwin use for his view that species share common ancestors and change over time, giving a tree of related life?
cards.body:
Descent with modification.

All species descend from **common ancestors**, and over generations their traits diverge, producing both unity (shared features) and diversity of life.

Key idea: Darwin proposed **natural selection** as the main mechanism of this change.
cards.searchQuery: descent with modification Darwin common ancestry meaning

cards.title: In what year did Darwin publish On the Origin of Species?
cards.body:
1859.

The book argued that species change through **natural selection** and share common ancestry, supported by evidence from fossils, geography, anatomy and artificial breeding.

Watch out: do not confuse the voyage of the Beagle (1831–1836) with the book's publication date.
cards.searchQuery: On the Origin of Species published year 1859 Darwin

cards.title: Which naturalist independently developed a theory of natural selection and sent Darwin a manuscript in 1858?
cards.body:
Alfred Russel Wallace.

Working in the Malay Archipelago, Wallace reached ideas very similar to Darwin's. Their joint papers were presented in **1858**, before Darwin's book appeared.

Tip: link Darwin with the Galápagos and Wallace with Southeast Asia.
cards.searchQuery: Alfred Russel Wallace natural selection 1858 Darwin

cards.title: Lamarck proposed that traits acquired during life, like a giraffe stretching its neck, are passed to offspring. What is this idea called?
cards.body:
Inheritance of acquired characteristics.

It is wrong: changes in body cells from use or disuse are generally **not passed on** through the germ line to offspring.

Watch out: natural selection works on existing **heritable** variation. Individuals don't evolve by trying to adapt.
cards.searchQuery: Lamarck inheritance of acquired characteristics vs natural selection

cards.title: Humans bred wild mustard into broccoli, cabbage and kale by choosing plants with desired traits. What process is this?
cards.body:
Artificial selection.

Humans, rather than the environment, choose which individuals reproduce. It shows how much **heritable variation** a species holds and how quickly selection can change it.

Key idea: Darwin used breeders' results as an analogy for natural selection.
cards.searchQuery: artificial selection wild mustard broccoli kale selective breeding

cards.title: What do we call a heritable trait that enhances an organism's fitness in a particular environment?
cards.body:
An adaptation.

Adaptations arise over generations as natural selection favors individuals with these traits. They are tied to a **specific environment**, so a trait that helps in one habitat may not in another.

Watch out: an individual's tan or larger muscles after training are not evolutionary adaptations, because they are not inherited.
cards.searchQuery: adaptation definition heritable trait enhances fitness

cards.title: Does natural selection produce new traits in direct response to what a population needs?
cards.body:
No: it sorts **existing variation**.

Mutations arise randomly with respect to need. Selection then favors the variants that happen to give higher survival and reproduction in the current environment.

Watch out: selection has no foresight, and what is favored today can be disfavored if the environment changes.
cards.searchQuery: natural selection acts on existing variation mutations random not directed

cards.title: Selection acts directly on which: an individual's genotype or its phenotype?
cards.body:
Phenotype.

Survival and reproduction depend on the **traits an organism displays**. Selection changes allele frequencies only indirectly, through the genotypes that produce favored phenotypes.

Watch out: a recessive allele hidden in heterozygotes is shielded from selection, because carriers show the dominant phenotype.
cards.searchQuery: natural selection acts on phenotype not genotype

cards.title: What is the ultimate source of new alleles in a population?
cards.body:
Mutation.

A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence. Only mutations in cells that form **gametes** can be passed to offspring.

Watch out: mutations are random with respect to the organism's needs, and most that affect fitness are harmful or neutral.
cards.searchQuery: ultimate source of genetic variation new alleles mutation

cards.title: Name three processes in sexual reproduction that shuffle existing alleles into new combinations.
cards.body:
Crossing over, independent assortment of chromosomes, and random fertilization.

These generate new **combinations** of alleles in offspring, but they do not create new alleles. That is the job of mutation.

Key idea: this shuffling is the reason siblings (except identical twins) differ genetically.
cards.searchQuery: sexual reproduction genetic variation crossing over independent assortment random fertilization

cards.title: How does antibiotic use lead to a population of resistant bacteria, such as MRSA?
cards.body:
It selects for resistance alleles that already exist by chance.

The antibiotic kills most sensitive cells, but rare **resistant** cells survive and reproduce. Their offspring dominate the next generation, so resistance becomes common.

Watch out: the drug doesn't cause the resistance mutations. It only changes who survives.
cards.searchQuery: antibiotic resistance natural selection MRSA how bacteria evolve

cards.title: Tiktaalik, from about 375 million years ago, had fish features such as fins and scales plus a neck and limb-like bones. What kind of fossil is it?
cards.body:
A transitional fossil.

It shows a mix of features from an ancestral group (fish) and a descendant group (**tetrapods**), documenting how the land vertebrate body plan arose.

Key idea: transitional fossils are predictions of evolution that have been found where expected in the rock record.
cards.searchQuery: Tiktaalik transitional fossil fish to tetrapod

cards.title: Fossils such as Pakicetus and Ambulocetus, together with DNA data, show whales descended from which group of land mammals?
cards.body:
Even-toed ungulates (artiodactyls).

The fossils show a series of forms with shrinking hind limbs and shifting ear and skull features. DNA data place whales among the artiodactyls, with **hippos** as their closest living relatives.

Key idea: whale pelvic and hind limb remnants are vestigial structures.
cards.searchQuery: whale evolution fossils Pakicetus Ambulocetus artiodactyls hippos

cards.title: What is the study of the geographic distribution of species called, which shows that island species resemble those on the nearest mainland?
cards.body:
Biogeography.

Island species tend to resemble species on the nearest continent more than species in similar habitats elsewhere. This fits **descent from colonizers** that then diverged.

Example: Galápagos finches are most similar to a South American ancestor.
cards.searchQuery: biogeography evidence for evolution island species resemble mainland

cards.title: Early embryos of fish, birds and humans all have pharyngeal pouches and a tail. What does this suggest?
cards.body:
A common vertebrate ancestry.

These features are **homologous** developmental structures. They develop into different parts in different groups, such as gills in fish and parts of the ear and throat in mammals.

Watch out: embryos do not literally repeat adult ancestral forms. They share early developmental pathways.
cards.searchQuery: embryology homology pharyngeal pouches vertebrate embryos common ancestry

cards.title: Why is it significant that nearly all organisms use essentially the same genetic code?
cards.body:
It is evidence that all life descends from a common ancestor.

The same codons specify the same amino acids in bacteria, plants and animals. A code that arbitrary is unlikely to arise **independently** many times.

Key idea: DNA and protein sequence comparisons give the strongest, most detailed evidence of evolutionary relationships.
cards.searchQuery: universal genetic code evidence common ancestry molecular homology

cards.title: If species X's DNA sequence for a gene is more similar to species Y's than to Z's, what does this suggest about their relationships?
cards.body:
X and Y likely share a more recent common ancestor.

Over time, lineages accumulate **different mutations**. The longer two lineages have been separate, the more their sequences generally differ.

Watch out: similar sequences suggest relatedness, but one gene alone can mislead, so biologists compare many genes.
cards.searchQuery: DNA sequence similarity relatedness common ancestor molecular evidence

cards.title: Sugar gliders (marsupials) and flying squirrels (placentals) look alike and both glide. What process explains this resemblance?
cards.body:
Convergent evolution.

Unrelated lineages facing **similar environmental challenges** evolve similar traits independently. Their gliding structures are analogous, not homologous.

Example: Australian marsupial mammals evolved forms resembling placental wolves, moles and anteaters elsewhere.
cards.searchQuery: convergent evolution sugar glider flying squirrel analogous

cards.title: In industrial England, dark peppered moths became common where soot darkened trees. What selective agent favored them?
cards.body:
Predation by birds.

On soot-darkened trees, light moths were more visible and eaten more often. **Camouflage** thus favored dark moths there. When pollution fell, light moths became common again.

Key idea: this is a classic case of directional selection tracking an environmental change.
cards.searchQuery: peppered moth industrial melanism bird predation camouflage

cards.title: What is the term for chance events that cause allele frequencies to fluctuate unpredictably from one generation to the next?
cards.body:
Genetic drift.

By luck, some individuals leave more offspring than others, so allele frequencies change **at random**, not because the alleles help.

Watch out: drift is not adaptive. It can even eliminate a beneficial allele or fix a harmful one.
cards.searchQuery: genetic drift definition random change allele frequencies

cards.title: Is genetic drift a stronger force in small populations or in large populations?
cards.body:
Small populations.

Chance deviations from expected allele frequencies are **proportionally larger** when few individuals reproduce, just as a few coin flips stray from 50% heads more than thousands do.

Key idea: in large populations, drift is weak and selection usually dominates.
cards.searchQuery: genetic drift stronger in small populations why

cards.title: Over time, does genetic drift tend to increase or decrease genetic variation within a single population?
cards.body:
It decreases it.

Drift can cause alleles to be **lost** or to become **fixed** (reach a frequency of 1), leaving fewer alleles in the population.

Key idea: across separate populations, drift makes them differ from one another, as different alleles are lost in each.
cards.searchQuery: genetic drift reduces genetic variation within populations fixation

cards.title: A disaster sharply cuts a population's size, and the survivors' alleles don't match the original gene pool. What is this called?
cards.body:
The bottleneck effect.

The survivors are a **random sample** of the original population, so some alleles may be lost and others over-represented, and variation falls.

Example: northern elephant seals, hunted down to a few dozen individuals in the 1890s, still have very low genetic variation even though their numbers have rebounded to well over $100{,}000$.
cards.searchQuery: bottleneck effect genetic drift northern elephant seals

cards.title: Of genetic drift, gene flow and natural selection, which one consistently leads to adaptation to the environment?
cards.body:
Natural selection.

Only selection **favors alleles** that improve fit to the environment. Drift and gene flow can change allele frequencies, but not in a way that systematically improves fitness.

Key idea: all three change allele frequencies and so cause evolution, but only one produces adaptive change.
cards.searchQuery: natural selection only mechanism consistently causing adaptive evolution

cards.title: Why is new mutation, acting alone, usually a weak force for changing allele frequencies within a population?
cards.body:
Mutation rates per gene per generation are very low.

A single new allele starts at a **tiny frequency**, so mutation alone changes allele frequencies slowly. Its essential role is supplying new variation for selection and drift to act on.

Watch out: weak as a direct force does not mean unimportant: without mutation, evolution would run out of raw material.
cards.searchQuery: mutation weak evolutionary force allele frequency low mutation rate

cards.title: What name is given to selection that maintains two or more alleles at a locus in a population over time?
cards.body:
Balancing selection.

It keeps **polymorphism** in a population. Two common forms are heterozygote advantage and frequency-dependent selection.

Key idea: it contrasts with directional selection, which tends to drive one allele to fixation.
cards.searchQuery: balancing selection maintains genetic polymorphism heterozygote advantage

cards.title: In malaria regions, carriers of one sickle-cell allele are more resistant to malaria than either homozygote. What is this called?
cards.body:
Heterozygote advantage.

Heterozygotes have higher fitness than **both** homozygotes, so both alleles persist. Normal homozygotes are more prone to malaria, and sickle-cell homozygotes suffer severe sickle-cell disease.

Key idea: it is a form of balancing selection.
cards.searchQuery: heterozygote advantage sickle cell malaria balancing selection

cards.title: A phenotype is favored only while it is rare, so its frequency tends to bounce back toward balance. What kind of selection is this?
cards.body:
Negative frequency-dependent selection.

Fitness of a phenotype **falls as it becomes common**, so neither form can take over. This keeps both in the population.

Example: in scale-eating cichlids in Lake Tanganyika, prey fish guard against the more common mouth-side morph, so the rarer morph succeeds.
cards.searchQuery: negative frequency-dependent selection scale-eating cichlids rare phenotype

cards.title: Male elephant seals fight for control of a harem of females. What form of sexual selection is this?
cards.body:
Intrasexual selection.

**Individuals of one sex**, usually males, compete directly for mates. The winners father more offspring.

Example: it favors large body size, weapons such as antlers and aggression, which is why males are often larger than females in such species.
cards.searchQuery: intrasexual selection male competition elephant seals mates

cards.title: What term describes differences between males and females in secondary sexual characteristics such as size, color or ornaments?
cards.body:
Sexual dimorphism.

It is often the result of **sexual selection**, which favors traits that improve mating success.

Example: male peafowl have the elaborate tail while peahens do not.
cards.searchQuery: sexual dimorphism definition secondary sexual characteristics sexual selection

cards.title: How can a showy trait that lowers an animal's survival, like a heavy tail, still be favored by selection?
cards.body:
Its gain in mating success outweighs its cost in survival.

Selection favors traits that raise **lifetime reproductive success**, not those that maximize survival. A male that dies young but fathers many offspring still spreads his alleles.

Key idea: fitness counts offspring, not longevity.
cards.searchQuery: sexual selection costly traits survival vs mating success tradeoff

cards.title: What is genetic variation called that gives neither an advantage nor a disadvantage in survival and reproduction?
cards.body:
Neutral variation.

Selection does not act on it, so its frequency can change by **genetic drift** alone.

Example: many differences in noncoding DNA are neutral. They accumulate over time and are useful for estimating how related species are.
cards.searchQuery: neutral variation neutral mutations genetic drift fitness

cards.title: Why can a harmful recessive allele persist in a diploid population even though selection acts against it?
cards.body:
Heterozygotes carry it without showing the trait.

Only **homozygous recessive** individuals are exposed to selection, so most copies of a rare recessive allele sit in carriers and are hidden from it.

Watch out: eliminating a rare recessive allele by selection is very slow, because rare alleles are mostly in heterozygotes.
cards.searchQuery: recessive alleles persist heterozygous carriers hidden from selection diploidy

cards.title: Name three reasons natural selection cannot produce perfect organisms.
cards.body:
Historical constraints, tradeoffs, and chance, along with a changing environment.

Selection can only modify **existing structures** and variation, and adaptations often trade off against each other. Chance events and environmental shifts also limit what evolves.

Example: a trait that speeds an animal up may make it more conspicuous to predators.
cards.searchQuery: limits of natural selection evolutionary constraints tradeoffs imperfect adaptations

cards.title: What is a graded change in a trait or allele frequency along a geographic transect called?
cards.body:
A cline.

Clines often reflect **environmental gradients**, such as temperature or altitude, where selection favors different phenotypes in different places.

Key idea: gene flow between neighboring populations makes the change gradual instead of abrupt.
cards.searchQuery: cline definition geographic gradient allele frequency trait

cards.title: Mating among close relatives raises the chance that offspring are homozygous for harmful recessive alleles. What is the resulting fitness loss called?
cards.body:
Inbreeding depression.

Relatives share many alleles, so their offspring are more often **homozygous**, which exposes rare harmful recessives.

Example: small, isolated populations, such as endangered species, are especially prone to it.
cards.searchQuery: inbreeding depression homozygous harmful recessive alleles small populations

cards.title: What is the total collection of alleles at all gene loci in all members of a population called?
cards.body:
The gene pool.

The **gene pool** of a population is what evolves: changes in its allele frequencies from generation to generation define microevolution.

Key idea: individuals don't evolve. A population's allele frequencies do.
cards.searchQuery: gene pool definition alleles population microevolution

cards.title: What is it called when two or more distinct forms of a trait, like red and white flowers, coexist in a population at appreciable frequencies?
cards.body:
Polymorphism.

Each form is called a **morph**. Polymorphism is maintained by processes such as balancing selection, or it may be transient while one form replaces another.

Watch out: do not confuse it with polyploidy, which is having extra chromosome sets.
cards.searchQuery: polymorphism definition morphs population variation biology

cards.title: What is the process called by which one species splits into two or more species?
cards.body:
Speciation.

It occurs when gene flow between populations is reduced enough that they diverge, and **reproductive isolation** evolves between them.

Key idea: speciation links microevolution (changes within populations) to macroevolution (the history of life's diversity).
cards.searchQuery: speciation definition one species splits reproductive isolation

cards.title: Which species concept defines species by measurable structural features, and can be applied to fossils and asexual organisms?
cards.body:
The morphological species concept.

It groups organisms by **shape and structure**. It can be used on fossils, asexual organisms and any case where interbreeding can't be observed.

Watch out: it depends on subjective judgment of which differences matter, and some species look alike.
cards.searchQuery: morphological species concept definition fossils asexual organisms

cards.title: Which species concept defines a species by its ecological niche, the way it interacts with the living and nonliving parts of its environment?
cards.body:
The ecological species concept.

It emphasizes **niche differences** and the selection pressures they create. It works for both sexual and asexual organisms.

Example: two bacterial populations using different resources could be classed as different species even though they never interbreed.
cards.searchQuery: ecological species concept niche definition

cards.title: Which species concept defines a species as the smallest group of individuals sharing a common ancestor, forming one branch on the tree of life?
cards.body:
The phylogenetic species concept.

It relies on **evolutionary history**, usually shown by morphological or DNA evidence. Applying it requires deciding how much divergence marks a separate species.

Key idea: it can be used for sexual and asexual organisms alike.
cards.searchQuery: phylogenetic species concept definition smallest monophyletic group

cards.title: What name is given to reproductive barriers that block mating or prevent fertilization of the egg?
cards.body:
Prezygotic barriers.

They act **before a zygote forms**. The five types are habitat, temporal, behavioral, mechanical and gametic isolation.

Mnemonic: HTB-MG, or "Hunters Tend to Be Mechanical Guys".
cards.searchQuery: prezygotic barriers types habitat temporal behavioral mechanical gametic

cards.title: Two garter snake species live in the same region, but one lives mostly in water and the other on land, so they rarely meet. Which barrier is this?
cards.body:
Habitat isolation.

Populations that occupy **different habitats** in the same area seldom encounter each other, even though no physical barrier separates them.

Key idea: it is a prezygotic barrier because it prevents mating before fertilization.
cards.searchQuery: habitat isolation garter snakes aquatic terrestrial prezygotic barrier

cards.title: Eastern and western meadowlarks overlap in range, but each responds only to its own species' song. Which barrier is this?
cards.body:
Behavioral isolation.

Courtship signals such as songs, displays or pheromones are **species-specific**, so individuals ignore other species' signals.

Example: male blue-footed boobies only court females that respond to their characteristic foot display.
cards.searchQuery: behavioral isolation meadowlarks songs prezygotic barrier

cards.title: Two snail species have shells coiled in opposite directions, so their genital openings don't line up and they can't mate. Which barrier is this?
cards.body:
Mechanical isolation.

Differences in **body structure** prevent successful copulation or pollen transfer.

Example: flower shape can match only certain pollinators, so pollen of one plant species isn't carried to another.
cards.searchQuery: mechanical isolation snail shell coiling flower structure prezygotic

cards.title: Sperm of one sea urchin species can't fertilize eggs of another, because their surface proteins don't recognize each other. Which barrier is this?
cards.body:
Gametic isolation.

Even when gametes meet, **molecular incompatibility** prevents the sperm and egg from fusing.

Example: in animals with external fertilization, such as sea urchins, species-specific binding proteins keep different species from fertilizing each other's eggs.
cards.searchQuery: gametic isolation sea urchin sperm egg recognition prezygotic

cards.title: A hybrid zygote forms but fails to develop or dies before reaching reproductive age. Which postzygotic barrier is this?
cards.body:
Reduced hybrid viability.

Genes from the two parent species can interact **incompatibly** during development, so hybrids die or are frail.

Key idea: it is postzygotic, because it acts after the hybrid zygote has formed.
cards.searchQuery: reduced hybrid viability postzygotic barrier hybrid inviability

cards.title: First-generation hybrids between two species are vigorous and fertile, but their offspring are weak or sterile. Which postzygotic barrier is this?
cards.body:
Hybrid breakdown.

The first generation (F1) survives and reproduces, but **later generations** (F2 and beyond) show reduced viability or fertility.

Example: some cultivated rice strains produce fertile F1 hybrids whose offspring are small and sterile.
cards.searchQuery: hybrid breakdown postzygotic barrier F2 hybrids sterile weak

cards.title: Why does geographic isolation promote divergence between populations of one species?
cards.body:
Gene flow between them stops.

Each isolated population then accumulates its own **mutations**, and drift and local selection act independently, so the populations grow apart genetically.

Key idea: allopatric speciation is complete once divergence produces reproductive isolation, even if the groups later meet again.
cards.searchQuery: allopatric speciation geographic isolation gene flow stops divergence

cards.title: Rhagoletis flies that mate and lay eggs on apples are diverging from those that use hawthorns, even though their ranges overlap. What mode of speciation is this?
cards.body:
Sympatric speciation.

A shift to a **new host plant** led to flies that mate on that plant and so are partly isolated, with no geographic barrier.

Watch out: this case is regarded as speciation in progress, not as a completed split.
cards.searchQuery: Rhagoletis apple maggot fly sympatric speciation hawthorn

cards.title: Why is sympatric speciation generally harder to achieve than allopatric speciation?
cards.body:
Gene flow between diverging groups continues.

When populations share the same area, **interbreeding** tends to mix their alleles and undo divergence unless strong selection or an instant barrier such as polyploidy prevents it.

Key idea: this is why polyploidy in plants is such a clean route to sympatric speciation.
cards.searchQuery: why sympatric speciation difficult gene flow counteracts divergence

cards.title: What is the name for a region where members of two different species meet and mate, producing at least some hybrid offspring?
cards.body:
A hybrid zone.

Hybrid zones act as **natural laboratories** for studying how reproductive barriers work and how species form or merge.

Example: fire-bellied and yellow-bellied toads in Europe form a hybrid zone, and most of their hybrids have reduced fitness.
cards.searchQuery: hybrid zone definition two species meet and mate hybrids

cards.title: What are the three possible outcomes when diverged populations meet in a hybrid zone?
cards.body:
Reinforcement, fusion, or stability.

Which outcome occurs depends on whether hybrids are **less fit**, equally fit, or intermediate in fitness.

Key idea: reinforcement strengthens barriers, fusion merges the species, and stability means hybrids persist in a narrow zone over time.
cards.searchQuery: hybrid zone outcomes reinforcement fusion stability

cards.title: When hybrids are less fit, selection can strengthen prezygotic barriers between the parent populations. What is this process called?
cards.body:
Reinforcement.

Individuals that **avoid mating with the other species** leave more offspring of normal fitness, so barriers to hybridization become stronger over generations.

Key idea: reinforcement can complete the speciation process in a hybrid zone.
cards.searchQuery: reinforcement speciation hybrid zone prezygotic barriers strengthen

cards.title: If reproductive barriers between two species weaken and hybrids are fit, the two may merge back into one. What is this outcome called?
cards.body:
Fusion.

Gene flow between the two groups increases until their **gene pools blend** and they become a single species.

Example: increased hybridization among cichlid fishes in Lake Victoria, when murky water hid color cues used in mate choice, has been linked to species loss.
cards.searchQuery: species fusion hybrid zone barriers weaken cichlids Lake Victoria

cards.title: Which term describes the splitting of one lineage into two or more lineages, as opposed to anagenesis, change within a single lineage?
cards.body:
Cladogenesis.

It is **branching evolution** and is the process that produces diversity by adding new species. Anagenesis changes a lineage over time without adding species.

Tip: "clado-" means branch, the same root as in cladogram.
cards.searchQuery: cladogenesis vs anagenesis branching evolution

cards.title: Why are prezygotic barriers generally considered more efficient than postzygotic barriers for the parents?
cards.body:
They prevent wasted reproductive effort.

Prezygotic barriers stop mating or fertilization, so parents don't spend **gametes, energy or parental care** on hybrids that are unfit or sterile.

Key idea: this is why selection against hybrids can strengthen prezygotic barriers (reinforcement).
cards.searchQuery: prezygotic vs postzygotic barriers wasted reproductive effort hybrids

cards.title: What is a branching diagram that represents a hypothesis about the evolutionary relationships among groups of organisms called?
cards.body:
A phylogenetic tree.

It shows **common ancestry** and the order of branching, not how advanced or similar the groups are in appearance.

Watch out: a tree is a hypothesis built from morphological and molecular data, and can be revised with new evidence.
cards.searchQuery: phylogenetic tree definition evolutionary relationships hypothesis

cards.title: What is the two-part naming system, genus then species, as in Homo sapiens, called?
cards.body:
Binomial nomenclature.

The first word is the **genus** (capitalized) and the second the species epithet (lowercase). Both are italicized in print or underlined when handwritten.

Key idea: Linnaeus popularized it, and a species name is unique worldwide.
cards.searchQuery: binomial nomenclature genus species Linnaeus naming

cards.title: List the taxonomic ranks in order from broadest to most specific.
cards.body:
Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

Each rank is **nested inside** the one before it. Similar species share a genus, similar genera share a family, and so on.

Mnemonic: "Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup".
cards.searchQuery: taxonomic hierarchy domain kingdom phylum class order family genus species

cards.title: On a phylogenetic tree, what does a branch point (node) represent?
cards.body:
The most recent common ancestor of the lineages that split there.

Each node is a **divergence** in which one ancestral lineage splits into two descendant lineages.

Watch out: the tips are present-day (or extinct) groups, not ancestors of one another.
cards.searchQuery: phylogenetic tree branch point node common ancestor meaning

cards.title: What term refers to two groups that share an immediate common ancestor not shared by any other group on the tree?
cards.body:
Sister taxa.

They appear as **neighboring branches** that come from the same node.

Key idea: sister taxa are each other's closest relatives, even if one of them looks very different.
cards.searchQuery: sister taxa definition phylogenetic tree immediate common ancestor

cards.title: Which term describes a taxon that includes a common ancestor and all (and only) its descendants?
cards.body:
Monophyletic (a clade).

A clade can be cut from a tree with **one snip**. Valid taxa in cladistics are monophyletic.

Example: the group of all mammals is monophyletic, since it includes the ancestral mammal and every descendant.
cards.searchQuery: monophyletic group clade definition common ancestor all descendants

cards.title: What term describes a group that includes a common ancestor but leaves out some of its descendants?
cards.body:
Paraphyletic.

It is an **incomplete clade**. The traditional group "reptiles" is paraphyletic if birds, which descend from within it, are excluded.

Watch out: don't confuse it with polyphyletic, which lacks the common ancestor.
cards.searchQuery: paraphyletic group definition excludes some descendants reptiles birds

cards.title: What term describes a group whose members do not include their most recent common ancestor, such as a group of warm-blooded animals made of birds and mammals?
cards.body:
Polyphyletic.

The members are **unrelated by recent shared ancestry**, so the group was built on convergent traits. Such groups are rejected in modern classification.

Example: grouping birds and mammals as "warm-blooded animals" would be polyphyletic, since endothermy evolved independently in each.
cards.searchQuery: polyphyletic group definition lacks common ancestor convergent traits

cards.title: In building a phylogenetic tree, what is a species or group called that is closely related to the ingroup but diverged before the ingroup's common ancestor?
cards.body:
The outgroup.

Comparing the ingroup with an outgroup shows which characters are **ancestral** and which are derived (new) within the ingroup.

Example: to study mammal relationships, a lizard could serve as an outgroup.
cards.searchQuery: outgroup phylogenetic analysis ancestral vs derived characters

cards.title: What is the technical term for a similarity between species that arose through convergent evolution rather than shared ancestry?
cards.body:
Homoplasy.

Homoplastic traits mislead tree-building, because they look like **shared derived characters** but did not come from a common ancestor.

Example: the streamlined bodies of sharks and dolphins evolved independently.
cards.searchQuery: homoplasy convergent evolution similarity not shared ancestry

cards.title: Which principle prefers the phylogenetic tree that requires the fewest evolutionary changes to explain the data?
cards.body:
Maximum parsimony.

It applies Occam's razor: the **simplest explanation** is preferred, here the tree needing the fewest character changes.

Watch out: the simplest tree is not guaranteed to be correct, so biologists also use likelihood-based methods.
cards.searchQuery: maximum parsimony phylogenetic tree fewest changes Occam razor

cards.title: What tool uses the roughly steady rate at which some DNA sequences change to estimate when lineages diverged?
cards.body:
A molecular clock.

If a gene accumulates changes at a roughly constant average rate, the **number of differences** between two species indicates how long ago they diverged.

Watch out: rates vary among genes and lineages, so clocks are calibrated against fossils or other dated events.
cards.searchQuery: molecular clock divergence time mutation rate calibration fossils

cards.title: What is the movement of genes between organisms by means other than parent-to-offspring inheritance called?
cards.body:
Horizontal gene transfer.

It is common among prokaryotes and blurs the "tree" pattern, because genes can pass **between distant lineages**.

Example: antibiotic resistance genes spread between bacterial species this way.
cards.searchQuery: horizontal gene transfer definition prokaryotes tree of life

cards.title: Name the three domains of life.
cards.body:
Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

Bacteria and Archaea are **prokaryotes**. Eukarya includes all organisms with a nucleus: protists, plants, fungi and animals.

Key idea: DNA sequence data show Archaea are more closely related to Eukarya than to Bacteria.
cards.searchQuery: three domains of life Bacteria Archaea Eukarya relationships

cards.title: On a tree, species A and B share a common ancestor more recent than the one they share with C. Which pair is more closely related?
cards.body:
A and B.

Relatedness is read from **how recently** two lineages shared a common ancestor, not from how similar they look or how close their tips are on the page.

Tip: trace each pair back to the node where their lines meet. The pair with the more recent node is closer.
cards.searchQuery: reading phylogenetic tree relatedness most recent common ancestor

cards.title: Does rotating the branches at a node of a phylogenetic tree change the relationships it shows?
cards.body:
No.

A node is like a hinge. Rotating it changes the **left-right order** of tips but not who shares a common ancestor with whom.

Watch out: the order of species along the tips of a tree does not show who is more advanced.
cards.searchQuery: rotating nodes phylogenetic tree same relationships left to right order

cards.title: After $3$ half-lives of a radioactive isotope, what fraction of the original parent isotope remains?
cards.body:
$\tfrac{1}{8}$

Each half-life halves what is left: $\tfrac{1}{2} \to \tfrac{1}{4} \to \tfrac{1}{8}$.

Why: after $n$ half-lives the fraction left is $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$, and for $n=3$ this gives $\tfrac{1}{8}$, or $12.5\%$.
cards.searchQuery: radiometric dating half-life fraction remaining after three half-lives

cards.title: What is the half-life of carbon-14, in years (number only, nearest ten)?
cards.body:
$5730$

Because it is so short, carbon-14 can only date **organic remains** up to roughly $50{,}000$ years old, after which too little is left to measure.

Tip: older rocks and fossils are dated using isotopes with far longer half-lives, such as uranium-238.
cards.searchQuery: carbon-14 half-life 5730 years radiocarbon dating limit

cards.title: Which mass extinction, about 252 million years ago, was the most severe in Earth's history?
cards.body:
The Permian extinction (end-Permian).

An estimated 96% of marine animal species and a large share of land species disappeared. It is linked to massive **volcanic eruptions** in Siberia, which changed climate and ocean chemistry.

Key idea: it is the boundary between the Paleozoic and Mesozoic eras.
cards.searchQuery: Permian extinction 252 million years ago worst mass extinction

cards.title: The mass extinction that ended the non-avian dinosaurs about 66 million years ago is linked to an impact crater near which Mexican peninsula?
cards.body:
The Yucatán Peninsula (Chicxulub crater).

An asteroid impact threw debris into the atmosphere and cooled the climate. A thin worldwide layer of **iridium-rich** clay marks it.

Key idea: it opened the way for the diversification of mammals.
cards.searchQuery: Chicxulub crater Yucatan Peninsula Cretaceous extinction dinosaurs

cards.title: Hawaiian honeycreepers diversified from one colonizing ancestor into many species adapted to different niches. What is this process called?
cards.body:
Adaptive radiation.

Many species arise from a common ancestor and **adapt to different ecological roles**. It is common after mass extinctions or when colonizing isolated islands with open niches.

Example: Darwin's finches and Hawaiian silverswords.
cards.searchQuery: adaptive radiation Hawaiian honeycreepers Darwin finches definition

cards.title: Which family of master regulatory genes controls the layout of body parts along the head-to-tail axis, and has been conserved in animals?
cards.body:
Hox genes.

They specify **where structures develop** along the body axis. Small changes in when and where they are expressed can produce large changes in body form.

Key idea: this is a core idea of evolutionary developmental biology (evo-devo).
cards.searchQuery: Hox genes body plan evolution evo-devo homeotic

cards.title: What term describes a trait that evolved for one function and was later co-opted for a different function?
cards.body:
Exaptation.

The trait was already present when it took on a new role, so evolution works by **modifying existing structures**.

Example: feathers likely evolved before flight, perhaps for insulation or display, and were later used in flight.
cards.searchQuery: exaptation definition trait co-opted new function feathers

cards.title: What is the name for the burst of diversification in which most major animal body plans appear in the fossil record, beginning about 540 million years ago?
cards.body:
The Cambrian explosion.

Most modern **animal phyla** first appear in Cambrian rocks, together with the first animals with hard parts.

Watch out: "explosion" spans many millions of years, so it is rapid on a geologic scale, not a sudden event.
cards.searchQuery: Cambrian explosion 540 million years ago animal body plans fossils

cards.title: Name the supercontinent that formed about 300 million years ago and began to break apart about 200 million years ago.
cards.body:
Pangaea.

Its formation and **breakup** by continental drift affected climates and separated populations, shaping the distribution of life.

Example: the separation of land masses explains why marsupials diversified in isolated Australia.
cards.searchQuery: Pangaea supercontinent formation breakup continental drift evolution
